pos: n. (Gergely Szegedi, c. 1511–1569, Hungarian Reformed preacher at Debrecen and Nagyvarad, and a writer against the antitrinitarians)
etymology: Szegedi, Hungarian, of Szeged, the town on the Tisza; Gergely, the Hungarian form of Gregory, from Greek gregoreo, to watch, to be vigilant.
biblical_def: Gergely Szegedi was a Franciscan of Hungarian birth who was drawn to the Reformation, studied at Wittenberg, and served as preacher at Gyula, Debrecen and Nagyvarad in the years when the Hungarian church was passing from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession under the Turkish and Transylvanian partition of the kingdom. He is remembered for the second of his two fights. The first was with Rome, carried on from the pulpit; the second was with the antitrinitarians, who after 1565 made headway in Transylvania and the Partium under the protection of the prince's physician and the preaching of Ferenc David, and who had to be answered in Hungarian by men the common people would read. Szegedi wrote that answer, setting the eternal deity of the Son and the Spirit from the plain places of Scripture rather than from the schoolmen, and he stood with Peter Melius and the Debrecen party at the disputations where the two confessions parted for good. He died in 1569, the year before the great debate at Nagyvarad. His name belongs in the dictionary because the Hungarian Reformation's hardest hour was not its struggle with the Mass but its struggle for the Trinity, and the men who held that line in a language with almost no theological vocabulary of its own were doing original work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead; a heretic as one who holds an opinion repugnant to the established faith; and to confute as to disprove, to overthrow by argument.
webster_full: TRINITY, n. [L. trinitas.] The union of three persons in one Godhead, or the three persons of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost in one divine nature.
HERETIC, n. [Gr. to choose.] A person under any religion, but particularly the Christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
CONFUTE, v.t. [L. confuto.] To disprove; to prove to be false or defective; to overthrow by argument or evidence.
PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one who inculcates any thing with earnestness.
GODHEAD, n. Godship; deity; divinity; divine nature or essence; applied to the true God.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Debrecen and Nagyvarad preacher who wrote against the Transylvanian antitrinitarians in Hungarian, for readers who had no Latin.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is antitrinitarianism as it took hold in Transylvania after 1565: the denial that the Son and the Spirit are God in the same sense as the Father, taught by Ferenc David and organised by Giorgio Biandrata, and granted standing by the Diet of Torda. It is not a nuance within Christianity. “Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jo 2:22) is the apostle's own classification, and the dictionary keeps it. The modern descendants of this error—Unitarianism, and the liberal theology which keeps the word God and empties the word Son—stand under the same judgment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Szegedi himself. The principle to recover is that the Trinity is defended in the vernacular or it is not defended at all. Szegedi wrote in Hungarian because the men being misled read Hungarian. A church whose doctrine of God lives only in its ministers' Latin has already lost the argument in its own pews.

pos: n. (Andras Szkharosi Horvat, active 1542–1549, Hungarian Protestant preacher at Tallya and the sharpest verse satirist of the Hungarian Reformation)
etymology: Szkharosi, Hungarian, of Szkharos, now Sarkad; Horvat, Hungarian, a Croat; Andras, the Hungarian form of Andrew, from Greek aner, a man.
biblical_def: Andras Szkharosi Horvat was a friar who became a Protestant preacher at Tallya in the Hegyalja wine country, and who between 1542 and 1549 wrote a handful of long poems in Hungarian which are the fiercest things in the literature of the Hungarian Reformation. They are not hymns. They are indictments in verse, meant to be sung or recited to people who could not read, against the worship of images, the selling of masses, the pride of the clergy, the oppression of the peasant by the landlord, and the sins of the nation which, he said plainly, had brought the Turk upon it. He took the prophets as his model and did not soften the application: if Israel was carried away for idolatry and injustice, Hungary at Mohacs had been broken for the same causes, and the remedy was repentance and not a crusade. The poems were printed at Krakow in the collection of Gal Huszar's circle and were read for a century. Nothing is known of his death. The dictionary keeps him for his method. He is the clearest Hungarian case of the Reformation preached in the common tongue, in the common measure, to people who owned no book—and of national calamity read, in the prophets' manner, as the judgment of God upon a people's sin rather than as mere misfortune.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a satire as a discourse exposing vice or folly; a plague as any great natural evil or calamity; and to reprove as to blame, to chide to the face.
webster_full: SATIRE, n. [L. satira.] A discourse or poem in which wickedness or folly is exposed with severity; keenness and severity of remark.
PLAGUE, n. [L. plaga, a stroke.] Any thing troublesome or vexatious; a pestilence; any great natural evil or calamity.
REPROVE, v.t. [L. reprobo.] To blame; to censure; to chide to the face; to charge with a fault.
IDOLATRY, n. [Gr. idol, and service.] The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.
VERSE, n. [L. versus.] A line consisting of a certain succession of sounds and number of syllables; metrical language.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Hab 2:18
What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?
corruption_summary: Hungarian verse satirist who named image worship, clerical greed and the oppression of the peasant as the sins for which God had given the kingdom to the Turk.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption he attacked was image worship, and the dictionary names it with him. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) is the second commandment, and the medieval church had not abolished it so much as explained it away by distinguishing the honour paid to the image from the worship due to God—a distinction the common people never made and were not meant to make, since the images were credited with the cures. Szkharosi wrote for those people and used their own measure to tell them what the commandment said.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophetic reading of national disaster. Modern writing on Mohacs treats the catastrophe as a matter of artillery, alliances and Habsburg politics, and so it was; Szkharosi insisted that it was also the hand of God upon a people, which is what every prophet says about every such defeat. The dictionary holds both: secondary causes are real, and they are the instruments of a providence that is moral.

pos: n. (Janos Apaczai Csere, 1625–1659, Transylvanian schoolman, author of the Hungarian Encyclopaedia, rector of the college of Kolozsvar)
etymology: Apaczai, Hungarian, of Apaca, his native village in the Barcasag; Csere, Hungarian, an oak-wood; Janos, the Hungarian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Janos Apaczai Csere was born in a Szekely village, educated at Kolozsvar and Gyulafehervar, and sent in 1648 to the Netherlands, where he studied at Franeker, Leiden and Utrecht, married a Dutch wife, and took the doctorate. He came home in 1653 convinced of three things which together made him the most important Hungarian schoolman of the century: that his people must be taught in Hungarian, that the sciences must be taught whole and not as a Latin ornament, and that the Reformed religion required an educated laity and not merely an educated clergy. His Hungarian Encyclopaedia of 1655 was the first attempt to set out the whole body of learning—logic, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, physics, agriculture, medicine, theology—in the Hungarian tongue, and he had to invent much of the vocabulary as he went. His inaugural address on the education of a people is a lament over Hungarian backwardness and an argument that it is remediable. He was made rector at Kolozsvar in 1656 and died there in 1659, aged thirty-four. The dictionary keeps him as the Hungarian answer to a question the Reformation raised everywhere: if every man is to read the Scriptures for himself, who will teach him to read, and in what language, and who will pay for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an encyclopedia as the circle of sciences; education as the bringing up and instruction of children; and the mother tongue as the native language of a people.
webster_full: ENCYCLOPEDIA, n. [Gr. in, a circle, and instruction.] The circle of sciences; a work in which the various branches of human knowledge are explained in alphabetical order.
EDUCATION, n. [L. educatio.] The bringing up, as of a child; instruction; formation of manners; comprehending all that series of instruction which is intended to enlighten the understanding.
TONGUE, n. The whole sum of words used by a particular nation; a language; the speech of a country.
VERNACULAR, adj. [L. vernaculus.] Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular language.
RECTOR, n. The head master of a school or college; a governor; a ruler.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: Transylvanian rector whose Hungarian Encyclopaedia of 1655 set out the whole body of learning in Hungarian, inventing the vocabulary as he went.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of Apaczai as a nationalist hero of the mother tongue with the religion left out. He did not argue for Hungarian instruction out of national sentiment but because the Reformed doctrine of Scripture requires a reading people, and a reading people must be taught in the language it actually speaks. Detach the argument from its premise and you keep the vernacular school and lose the reason for it.

The principle to recover is the one Nehemiah's Levites practised: “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Reading aloud is not enough; the sense must be given, and given in a tongue the hearer owns. A church which will not fund the teaching of its children has not understood its own doctrine of the sufficiency of Scripture, since a sufficient book is no use to a man who cannot read it.

pos: n. (Pal Medgyesi, 1604–1663, court chaplain at Sarospatak and the chief writer of the Hungarian Puritan party)
etymology: Medgyesi, Hungarian, of Medgyes, now Mediasi in Transylvania; Pal, the Hungarian form of Paul, from Latin paulus, small.
biblical_def: Pal Medgyesi studied at Debrecen and then in England at Cambridge, which few Hungarians of his generation did, and came home carrying the English practical divinity with him. He was chaplain to Susanna Lorantffy, the princess of Transylvania, and preacher at Sarospatak, where her court made the nearest thing Hungary had to a Puritan centre. He translated Lewis Bayly's Practice of Piety into Hungarian in 1636 and it went through many editions; it taught a nation of Reformed hearers how a Christian orders a day, a household and a death-bed. He went on to argue in print for presbyterian church government—ruling elders, graded assemblies, discipline exercised by the congregation's officers rather than by a bishop and his archdeacons—and in this he was opposed and defeated by Istvan Geleji Katona and the episcopal order of the Transylvanian church. His later works are mostly laments: funeral sermons for the house of Rakoczi and jeremiads over the ruin of Transylvania after the disastrous Polish campaign of 1657. He died in 1663. The dictionary keeps him because he is the point at which the English Puritan movement reached Hungary, and because his argument for presbyterian order, though it lost in his own synod, is substantially the order the dictionary holds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines piety as reverence of God with obedience; a chaplain as a clergyman who performs divine service in a family; and discipline as instruction and government, as in a church.
webster_full: PIETY, n. [L. pietas.] Reverence of God and his character and laws; godliness; the practice of the duties of religion, proceeding from love and reverence.
CHAPLAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who performs divine service in a family, in a ship, or in an army.
DISCIPLINE, n. [L. disciplina.] Instruction and government; subjection to laws, rules and order; correction; chastisement.
PRESBYTERY, n. [Gr. an elder.] A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of the ministers and elders of churches in a district.
LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
scriptures: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Rom 5:3
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
corruption_summary: Sarospatak court chaplain who brought the English practical divinity into Hungarian and argued, unsuccessfully, for presbyterian order in the Transylvanian church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine controversy is the one he lost, and the dictionary states its side. Medgyesi held that the New Testament knows ruling elders in every congregation and graded assemblies above them, and that a superintendent with ordinary jurisdiction over other presbyters has no warrant. “the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) is his text and it is a good one. The dictionary holds congregational government with a plurality of elders, which is nearer Medgyesi than Geleji Katona, and names the Transylvanian episcopate as a prudential arrangement the New Testament does not require.

The principle to recover is that church order is a matter of warrant and not of convenience. Geleji Katona's case was that a Hungary surrounded by Turks and Habsburgs needed strong superintendence, and the case was practically strong. But the regulative principle asks what Scripture commands, not what the emergency recommends, and a government adopted for an emergency has a way of outlasting it by three centuries.

pos: n. (Istvan Geleji Katona, 1589–1649, Reformed bishop of Transylvania and author of the Canones Ecclesiastici of 1649)
etymology: Geleji, Hungarian, of Gelej in Borsod; Katona, Hungarian, a soldier; Istvan, the Hungarian form of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, a crown.
biblical_def: Istvan Geleji Katona was trained at Heidelberg, served as court preacher at Gyulafehervar under Gabriel Bethlen, and from 1633 was superintendent, or bishop, of the Transylvanian Reformed church until his death. He was a considerable preacher and a considerable administrator, and his legacy is a book of church law. The Canones Ecclesiastici, drawn up under his hand and received by the synod of Szatmarnemeti in 1649, governed the Hungarian Reformed churches for two hundred years: it fixed the duties and the examination of ministers, the visitation of parishes, the schools, the marriage courts, the discipline of scandalous members, and the authority of the superintendent and his archdeacons. He wrote it in the teeth of the Puritan party, whose presbyterian proposals he regarded as a threat to the only structure holding a church together between the Turk and the Habsburg, and he used his office against them with a heavy hand. He also pressed, with real zeal, for preaching to the Romanians of Transylvania in their own tongue. The dictionary records both halves. A man may be right that a church needs order, discipline and law, and wrong about which order Scripture warrants; and a bishop who crushes a scruple instead of answering it has not strengthened the discipline he defends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law or rule of doctrine or discipline; a superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something; and visitation as the act of a superior who inspects his churches.
webster_full: CANON, n. [Gr. a rule.] In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by authority.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction; an overseer.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; particularly, the act of a superior or superintendent, who visits churches or schools to inspect their state.
ORDER, n. [L. ordo.] Regular disposition; settled mode of proceeding; established method; rule; the system of a church's government.
SCRUPLE, n. [L. scrupulus.] Doubt; hesitation concerning the decision of the mind on a question of right or duty.

For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
corruption_summary: Transylvanian Reformed bishop whose Canones Ecclesiastici of 1649 governed the Hungarian churches for two centuries, and who used his office to crush the Puritan party.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary's correction of Geleji Katona is confessional, not modern. His superintendency claimed an ordinary jurisdiction over other presbyters; the New Testament uses elder, bishop and overseer for one office, and “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) is a plurality in each place rather than a grade above them. The 1689 London Baptist Confession knows two offices, elder and deacon, and no third. His Canones are a monument of pastoral care and a monument of an order Scripture does not require.

The principle to recover is that discipline and liberty of conscience are not rivals. Geleji Katona treated the Puritan scruple as insubordination and silenced it, and the scruple came back in every generation afterwards. A church that cannot bear to have its polity questioned from Scripture is confessing that it does not expect the question to be answerable.

pos: n. (Gyorgy Martonfalvi Toth, 1635–1681, professor of theology at Debrecen and the chief Hungarian teacher of the Amesian divinity)
etymology: Martonfalvi, Hungarian, of Martonfalva, Martin's village; Toth, Hungarian, a Slovak; Gyorgy, the Hungarian form of George, from Greek georgos, a tiller of the earth.
biblical_def: Gyorgy Martonfalvi Toth studied at Debrecen and then at Utrecht and Franeker, and from 1659 taught at Debrecen, first in the great college and then, after the Turks burned Nagyvarad and its school fled to him, as the professor on whom the whole theological teaching of Reformed Hungary east of the Tisza rested. He taught out of the Medulla of William Ames, the English Puritan who had spent his last years at Franeker, and his own two volumes are an exposition of it: a tight, scholastic, practical divinity in which every doctrine is stated, proved from Scripture, defended against the adversary named, and then applied to conscience and duty. He published a Hungarian catechetical and logical textbook for his students, and he taught through the years when Debrecen was paying tribute to the Turk, sheltering refugees from the Habsburg counter-Reformation in Upper Hungary, and losing ministers to the galleys. He died in 1681. The dictionary keeps him because he is the plainest proof that a besieged church can still teach systematically. Hungarian Reformed theology did not survive the seventeenth century by lowering its standards; it survived by a professor in a frontier town working through the loci one at a time with students who might be arrested for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines divinity as the science of divine things; a system as a regular connected whole; and to apply as to put to use, to appropriate to a particular case.
webster_full: DIVINITY, n. [L. divinitas.] The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God and our relations and duties to him; theology.
SYSTEM, n. [Gr. to set together.] An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a connected scheme of doctrines or principles.
APPLY, v.t. [L. applico.] To lay on; to put to use; to appropriate to a particular case; as to apply a doctrine to the conscience.
MARROW, n. [Sax. mearh.] A soft oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of bones; hence, the best part or essence of a thing.
COLLEGE, n. [L. collegium.] A society of persons engaged in common pursuits; an edifice appropriated to the use of students acquiring learning.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Debrecen professor who taught the whole body of divinity out of William Ames while his province paid tribute to the Turk and lost ministers to the galleys.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of system in theology—the notion that the scholastic method of stating, proving, defending and applying a doctrine is a rationalist cage from which a biblical faith must be released. Martonfalvi is the answer. His system exists to get the doctrine to the conscience: the method ends in use, and the use is obedience. A theology without that frame does not become warmer; it becomes vague, and a vague doctrine cannot be defended by a man who may be arrested for it tomorrow.

The principle to recover is the order in the apostle's charge: “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), and then “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Study is for preaching, and preaching for the hearer's obedience. Debrecen's students learned the loci in a frontier town; what made the learning worth its cost was that they then went out and preached it under the Turk.

“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — students who might be arrested for the doctrine they learned.

pos: n. (Mihaly Tofeus, 1624–1684, court preacher and Reformed bishop of Transylvania, expositor of the Psalms)
etymology: Tofeus, a Latinised form of Hungarian Dobos, a drummer; Mihaly, the Hungarian form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, who is like God.
biblical_def: Mihaly Tofeus was born at Szatmar, studied at Debrecen and then for six years in the Netherlands and England, and returned to serve as professor at Nagyvarad and Sarospatak before becoming court preacher to Michael Apafi, prince of Transylvania, and in 1679 superintendent of the Transylvanian Reformed church. His one great book is a volume of expositions of the Psalms, preached before the prince and his court and taken down as he delivered them. It is a plain, severe, applicatory exposition, verse by verse, and it is remarkable for its candour: a court preacher who tells the prince, the councillors and the ladies in attendance what the psalm says about their own particular sins, by name and without softening, and who returns again and again to the ruin of Transylvania as the chastisement of a professing people. He was a hard man and his contemporaries said so. He died at Gyulafehervar in 1684, four years before the principality passed under Habsburg rule. The dictionary keeps him for the rarest thing in his office. A chaplain paid by a prince, preaching in the prince's hearing, who applies the text to the prince, is doing what Nathan did; and the Psalms, which are the prayers of a king who had been so dealt with, are the right book for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalm as a sacred song or hymn; exposition as explanation, interpretation; and to apply as to fix the mind on, to appropriate to a particular case.
webster_full: PSALM, n. [Gr. to touch, to strike, as a lyre.] A sacred song or hymn; a composition in verse intended to be sung in the worship of God.
EXPOSITION, n. [L. expositio.] Explanation; interpretation; a laying open of the sense or meaning of an author or of a text.
APPLY, v.t. To fix the mind on; to appropriate to a particular person or case; to use as suitable or relative.
COURT, n. The residence of a prince; the hall or chamber where a sovereign resides; the persons who compose the retinue of a sovereign.
CHASTISEMENT, n. Correction; punishment; pain inflicted for punishment and correction, either by a parent or by God.
scriptures: Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Rom 5:3
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
corruption_summary: Transylvanian court preacher and bishop whose Psalm expositions named the sins of the prince and the court to their faces.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the court chaplaincy that has forgotten what it is for—the preacher attached to power whose sermons comfort it. It is an ancient trade: Jeremiah had four hundred competitors in it. The test is simple and Tofeus passed it: does the man apply the text to the people who pay him. The dictionary notes also that he was severe beyond what charity required, and that severity in a pulpit is not the same thing as faithfulness, though it is often mistaken for it by the severe.

The principle to recover is the preacher's duty to the great. “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10) is addressed to rulers, and someone has to read it to them. Where the church flatters the magistrate it loses both its own soul and its usefulness to him, since a prince surrounded by agreement is a prince without information.

pos: n. (Istvan Bocskai, 1557–1606, prince of Transylvania, whose rising won the Peace of Vienna and its guarantee of Protestant worship)
etymology: Bocskai, Hungarian, of Bocska; Istvan, the Hungarian form of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, a crown or garland.
biblical_def: Istvan Bocskai was a Hungarian magnate who had served the Habsburgs faithfully and had helped bring Transylvania under the emperor's authority. He turned against them when the imperial government, having won the country, began to take it apart: treason trials used to confiscate the estates of Protestant nobles, the seizure of the great Lutheran church at Kassa for Roman worship, and a declared policy of restoring the old religion in Upper Hungary by the army. In 1604 the crown moved against Bocskai's own lands; he raised the Hajdu free-soldiers of the Tisza, was joined by the nobility and the Protestant towns, was elected prince of Transylvania and of Hungary, and fought the emperor to a standstill. He refused the crown the Turks offered him. The Peace of Vienna in 1606 conceded what the rising had been for: freedom of worship to the Protestant nobles, towns and garrison soldiers of Hungary, and the restoration of the Hungarian constitutional offices. He died within the year, probably poisoned. The dictionary records the settlement as a mercy and declines to make him a saint. His cause was the lawful defence of an estate's liberties against a sovereign breaking his own oath, which the Reformed political writers allowed; his army plundered friend and enemy alike, and the Hajdu were feared in Hungary for a century after.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint; a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with authority; and an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God.
webster_full: LIBERTY, n. [L. libertas.] Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, except as restrained by law; civil liberty is exemption from the arbitrary will of others.
MAGISTRATE, n. [L. magistratus.] A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it; a person clothed with power.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
PLUNDER, v.t. To pillage; to spoil; to strip of goods by open force, as in war.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: Prince of Transylvania whose rising of 1604 won at Vienna in 1606 the first legal guarantee of Protestant worship in Hungary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine question is the lawfulness of the rising, and the dictionary answers it on Reformed grounds rather than nationalist ones. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) is the rule, and it is not suspended by inconvenience. What the Reformed political writers allowed was narrower and is what happened here: lesser magistrates—the estates and the free towns, themselves ordained powers—defending in arms a constitution the sovereign had sworn to and was breaking. That is not private rebellion. The distinction matters, because without it every grievance becomes a warrant.

The principle to recover is that a toleration won by the sword is still only a toleration. The 1606 peace protected Protestant worship in Hungary for a century, and the dictionary thanks God for it; but the Hajdu who won it plundered the country, and the Counter-Reformation returned by patient legal means within two generations. Liberty of conscience is not finally secured by cavalry. “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7).

Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668) — deliverance, victory, safety; “but safety is of the LORD”, Proverbs 21:31.

“The horse is prepared against the day of battle” (Pro 21:31) — the Hajdu free-soldiers of the Tisza raised in 1604.
“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” (Psa 20:7) — the Peace of Vienna, 1606, and the Counter-Reformation's legal return.

pos: n. (Ferenc David, c. 1520–1579, Transylvanian preacher who denied the Trinity and founded the Hungarian antitrinitarian church)
etymology: David, a Hungarian surname from the Hebrew personal name Dawid, beloved; Ferenc, the Hungarian form of Francis, from Latin Franciscus, a Frank.
biblical_def: Ferenc David was born at Kolozsvar of a Saxon father, studied at Wittenberg, and rose through the Transylvanian church by stages that each left a confession behind him. He was Lutheran superintendent, then Reformed superintendent, and then, from about 1565, the leader of the party which denied that the Son and the Spirit are God. In this he was pushed and organised by Giorgio Biandrata, the Italian physician who was the prince's doctor and the ablest antitrinitarian politician in Europe. David preached the new doctrine in Kolozsvar, carried the city with him, disputed against Peter Melius and the Reformed at Nagyvarad in 1569, and secured the standing of his church under the toleration voted by the Diet of Torda. He then went further than his own party would follow: he taught that Christ is not to be invoked or worshipped at all, since he is only a man. Biandrata, alarmed, brought Faustus Socinus from Poland to argue him down; David would not yield, was tried by the Diet in 1579 for innovation, and died in prison at Deva the same year. The dictionary enters him as the Hungarian Reformation's most serious wound, inflicted from inside by a man who had three times subscribed a confession of the deity of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an antitrinitarian as one who denies the Trinity; apostasy as an abandonment of what one has professed; and to blaspheme as to speak impiously of God or sacred things.
webster_full: ANTITRINITARIAN, n. One who denies the Trinity, or the existence of three persons in the Godhead.
APOSTASY, n. [Gr. a defection.] An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
BLASPHEME, v.t. [Gr. to speak evil.] To speak of the Supreme Being in terms of impious irreverence; to revile or speak reproachfully of God.
WORSHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; religious reverence and homage.
INNOVATION, n. Change made by the introduction of something new; a novelty introduced into an established order.
scriptures: And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Heb 1:8
But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.
Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: Transylvanian superintendent who passed from Lutheran to Reformed to antitrinitarian, taught that Christ is not to be worshipped, and died in prison in 1579.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is itself the naming of a corruption, and the dictionary names it without hedging. The denial of the eternal deity of the Son is not a variant Christianity, an alternative reading or a point on which serious men may differ. It is the error the apostle calls by its name: “He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jo 2:22). Thomas's confession, “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28), was received by Christ rather than corrected, and the Father addresses the Son as God in Hebrews 1:8. David's final position—that Christ is not to be invoked—only drew out what the earlier position already contained, which is why Biandrata and Socinus, who had taught him the premise, were so anxious to disown the conclusion.

The line of this error runs forward, and should be traced rather than forgotten: Transylvanian antitrinitarianism and Polish Socinianism into English and New England Unitarianism, and from there into the liberal Protestantism which keeps the word God, keeps the word Christ, and means by the second a man uniquely filled with the first. The dictionary holds the Chalcedonian definition and the Nicene faith, and reads David's career as a warning that a confession three times subscribed is no security at all where the Scriptures are read for a system instead of heard as the voice of God.

pos: n. (Giorgio Biandrata, c. 1515–1588, Piedmontese physician who organised the antitrinitarian churches of Poland and Transylvania)
etymology: Biandrata, also written Blandrata, from the Piedmontese place Biandrate; Giorgio, the Italian form of George, from Greek georgos, a husbandman.
biblical_def: Giorgio Biandrata was a physician of Saluzzo in Piedmont who practised at the courts of Europe and used the freedom of a court doctor to carry a doctrine. He left Italy for Geneva, where Calvin suspected him at once and said so; he went to Poland and became the chief organiser of the antitrinitarian party among the nobility of the Lesser Poland churches; and from 1563 he was physician to the prince of Transylvania, where he found Ferenc David and made of him the preacher the movement needed. Biandrata himself wrote little under his own name. His gift was management: he placed men, drafted documents other men signed, procured the toleration voted at Torda, and kept the favour of two princes. When David pressed on to deny that Christ should be worshipped at all, Biandrata broke with him, brought Faustus Socinus from Poland to refute him, and took part in the proceedings which put his own protege in the prison where he died. He lived on in Transylvania until 1588. The dictionary enters him as the type of a particular danger: not the open heretic in a pulpit, who can be answered, but the patient, well-placed, personally agreeable man who never quite states the doctrine himself and simply arranges that it shall be taught.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a physician as a person skilled in the art of healing; intrigue as a plot or private scheme; and subtle as sly in design, artful, cunning.
webster_full: PHYSICIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases.
INTRIGUE, n. [L. intrico, to perplex.] A plot or scheme of a complicated nature; a private or secret scheme, usually for a selfish purpose.
SUBTLE, adj. [L. subtilis.] Sly in design; artful; cunning; insinuating; as a subtle foe.
PATRON, n. [L. patronus.] One who countenances, supports or protects; a defender; an advocate.
LEAVEN, n. [L. levo, to raise.] A mass of sour dough which, mixed with a larger quantity, produces fermentation in it; hence, that which makes a general change in the mass.
scriptures: But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: Piedmontese court physician who organised antitrinitarianism in Poland and Transylvania, and then helped destroy the preacher he had made.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is antitrinitarianism and the dictionary has named it in the entry on Ferenc David. What this entry adds is the method, which the apostle describes exactly: “who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1). Privily is the word. Biandrata did not arrive announcing a denial of the Son; he arrived as a physician with excellent manners, became useful to princes, placed sympathetic men in livings and chairs, and let the preaching be done by others. Calvin's early distrust of him was called uncharitable at the time, and was right.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of trying the spirits. “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1) is addressed to a congregation, not to a court of inquisition, and it assumes that error will come recommended. The test is doctrine stated plainly and examined, which is precisely what a man of Biandrata's sort will always find a reason to postpone. His use of David and then abandonment of him to the prison also stands as a judgment on the method: a movement held together by management eats its own preachers.
